extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, lexicography, and scientific terminology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how to formulate, fix, and evaluate definitions and connotations of terms used in science, philosophy, and common language, with attention to semantic drift, historical meaning, and pragmatic constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition as part of discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: “The business of definition is part of the business of discovery.... To define, so that our definition shall have any scientific value, requires no small portion of that sagacity by which truth is detected.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition should follow a genuine advance in knowledge; to define usefully one must have pretty well known what truth is to be stated. Definitions are not mere verbal fixes but steps in knowledge; avoid defining before the underlying phenomena are understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know all common properties and causal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to judge finally how the name which denotes a class may best be defined, we must know all the properties common to the class, and all the relations of causation or dependence among those properties.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A correct scientific definition requires surveying the class's shared properties and understanding causal/dependence relations so that the chosen connotation captures the essential structure of the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer obvious, familiar marks for definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: “If the properties which are fittest to be selected as marks... are also obvious and familiar, and especially if they bear a great part in producing that general air of resemblance... the definition will then be most felicitous.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, select as defining marks those properties that are evident and play a central role in perceived resemblance; these yield clearer, more usable definitions for common understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow non‑familiar properties when they are the best marks
rubrics_metrics.description: “But it is often necessary to define the class by some property not familiarly known, provided that property be the best mark of those which are known.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not shy from using a less obvious or technical property as the defining criterion if it does the best job of distinguishing the class (example: De Blainville's biological definition based on continuous decomposition/recomposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical flexibility when ideal definition impossible
rubrics_metrics.description: “Cases in which it is impossible to comply with all the conditions of a precise definition of a name in agreement with usage, occur very frequently.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when usage, ambiguity, or multiple derived senses make a single precise connotation impracticable; adapt definitions pragmatically rather than forcing an artificial precision that contradicts common use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and analyze transitive/derivative applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Words may acquire transitive or derivative applications by gradual extension from one set of objects to another, sometimes without a common property among all applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace the chain of associations that produced extended meanings (Stewart's transitive applications). Understanding whether extensions arise from universal human associations or chance local use helps assess whether a single definition is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish casual vs natural/habitual associations
rubrics_metrics.description: “Where the association is slight and casual, the several meanings will remain distinct... Where the association is so natural and habitual as to become virtually indissoluble, the transitive meanings will coalesce in one complex conception.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the strength of associative links: slight/casual links preserve distinct senses; deep/habitual links merge meanings. This informs whether to treat senses as separate or as one complex sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forcing a single genus across genuinely distinct meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical logicians erred by seeking a definition that would serve for several distinct meanings at once (e.g., attempts to find a common idea of 'cause').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to manufacture a single essential commonality when the phenomena genuinely lack one; recognize ambiguity and allow multiple senses rather than producing vacuous generalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restricting connotation over extending it when fixing vague terms
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is better, in such a case, to give a fixed connotation to the term by restricting, than by extending its use; rather excluding from the epithet... than leaving out of its connotation any of the qualities... the general mind may have been habitually guided.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When formalizing a vague or polysemous term, restrict its denotation to preserve salient, historically important meanings rather than enlarging it to include all agreeable applications (example: the term 'beautiful').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard previous connotations without deep justification
rubrics_metrics.description: “We must take care not to discard (unless advisedly, and on the ground of a deeper knowledge of the subject) any portion of the connotation which the word... previously carried with it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect language's role as conservator of past experience; loss of prior connotations can erase historical insights. Any deliberate change should be grounded in thorough knowledge and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use predication to keep meanings alive
rubrics_metrics.description: “The habit of predicating of the name, all the various properties which it originally connoted, keeps up the association between the name and those properties.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively assert or teach the predicates historically associated with a term to maintain their cognitive linkage; without such predication, complex meanings fade from common thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that words habitually call up only parts of their meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A word originally associated with a very complex cluster of ideas often calls up only one or two elements; otherwise thought would be too slow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that normal use triggers partial recall; when full precision matters, explicitly evoke the remaining parts of the complex meaning rather than relying on default associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of premature fixation of terms during periods of semantic decay
rubrics_metrics.description: When words have lost significance, persons aiming for definite language may fix the term at the diminished connotation, thereby extending its denotation beyond historical meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid formalizing definitions based on the impoverished understanding of an age; ensure the definers have access to the term's fuller historical sense, or risk freezing usage at a degraded level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the history of a word before redefining it
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whoever seeks to introduce a more correct use of a term... should be required to possess an accurate acquaintance with the history of the particular word, and of the opinions which in different stages of its progress it served to express.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scholars redefining terminology must survey prior uses and beliefs attached to the term; if a new definition would render formerly accepted propositions false, the redefinition must be justified and those cases addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer historical analysis over dictionary glosses for correct employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Dictionaries give a broad blunt meaning; the history of a word may show the law by which its successive meanings were produced and be a better guide to its employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When precise nuance matters, consult the historical development of a word rather than relying solely on dictionary definitions, because incidental associations often shape real usage beyond the dictionary entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the twin movements of generalization and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Language exhibits two counter-movements: Generalization (words lose portions of connotation and become more general) and Specialization (words acquire additional or altered connotation by restriction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate and analyze which direction a term's meaning is trending; this helps in choosing whether and how to intervene (e.g., fix connotation, allow natural drift, or reclaim lost senses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against degeneration of language through unskilled usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorant or superficial use of words by many new writers can extend loose usage and deprive language of valuable expressive modes; vulgarisms creep in and spoil precise expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain standards of education and careful written practice; editors and teachers should resist careless extensions of meaning and preserve valuable distinctions in usage.
